title: Why Own Your Intelligence? Harrison Chase Keynote | Interrupt London

segments.text: Welcome to Interrupt, everyone.
It's great to be here in London.
Last year, we just did Interrupt in San Francisco.
This year we're doing it in San Francisco, New York, and London.
So it's really great to be here in person with all of you talking about agents
and evals and all that fun stuff.
We have a great lineup for you today.
We've got a ton of fantastic speakers.
Some fireside chats, some deep dives on a lot of the cool technology
that we're building.
And I wanted to kick off the day with just kind of like an overview of how
we think of the state of agents and AI and some of the directions that we're
pushing in. Before talking about the future, though, I want to talk a little
bit about how we got here.
And so I want to...
I want to figure out how the clicker works.
There we go. And so I want to start in the year, kind of, 2023.
And so this is when LangChain was first getting started.
A lot of LangChain was around helping people build prototypes of agents because
that's what everyone was thinking about at the time.
It was super new, super exploratory.
And then in 2024, we started to see applications come online, but they
were simpler types of applications.
They were a single LLM call, a chain of LLM calls, chatbots.
And in 2025, we started to see that people were exploring agents for the first
time. But then really this past year, I feel like this has been the year that
agents have come alive and in particular started to transform the application
layer. So we've seen a ton of agents being built for vertical use cases
for different points in the application layer.
And the key part about all of these agents is they're not just an LLM.
They're driven by an LLM, of course, that's at the center, but the thing that
makes all of these application layer agents really take off and actually work
is everything around the LLM, the system around it.
And so we've seen a number of companies basically build these systems,
these harnesses around these LLMs.
And that's what's causing agents to work.
And so for some examples of this, you'll hear later today from Monday about
how they built their agent, and they built kind of this continual feedback
loop with evals and started improving in that direction.
Harvey is a great example of a customer who's done this, where they are fine-tuning
models for specialized tasks.
So again, it's not just the model, it's the system around it, including this
system for fine-tuning models.
And then Orange, you'll hear from them as well later today about how they built
this specialized harness with governance in it.
And governance is a key part of what makes this agent work.
So we're really seeing that it's not just the model, it's everything around
the model. It's the harness with skills, tools, context, controls,
governance. And when we see these agents start to come into production
and really transform what's happening, it's really everything around the
model. And because of this, like, specialization that is happening, you're taking
this model and then you're building the system around it that makes it really
really work for a particular domain that you're an expert in.
This is why we think it's so important to own your intelligence, because
that specialization is what really makes these agents work.
And when we think of that specialization at the harness layer,
at the model layer, at the context layer, when we think of that specialization,
to us, that's what it really means to own your intelligence.
And we're seeing like a few trends that are driving this desire to own
one's intelligence and the importance of owning one's intelligence.
One is just cost. So we're seeing AI tools get adopted more than
ever now. Cost therefore is increasing a lot.
And so if you're not in control of this whole agentic system in some
form, then the costs will get out of control.
We're seeing open models start to become more and more prevalent.
And so NVIDIA, Kimi, DeepSeek, all of these have released really performant
open-source and open-weight models that you can use for cheaper, but also
that you can post-train and really make specialized.
And then the third thing that we're seeing people realize, and this
is, I think, the biggest thing that's driving these, like, vertical agents
that are really having impact, is the impact that data can have.
So we're seeing that when you're creating a kind of like vertical, differentiated
experience, the data that you bring, the context that you bring, the knowledge
that you bring to shape the harness, that's what really differentiates it from
someone just using ChatGPT or using Claude.
And so our mission at LangChain is to enable every company to own their intelligence.
We think this is what's needed to give birth to thousands of
vertical or company-specific harnesses.
And we really want to help make this happen.
So what are the core pillars of that?
In our mind, there's three.
The first is open. And so this refers to the whole agent apparatus itself.
And so again, the model, the harness, and the context.
We think all of these need to be open.
When we talk about a model being open, yes, there are open-weight models, but
more than that, we really just mean model optionality.
Having the option to choose which model to use, whichever one's best, whichever
one's fastest, cheapest, best for your domain, you should have model optionality.
The harness should be open and controllable.
So when you think about shaping these general-purpose LLMs for your domain,
a big part of that is making them do things in a particular way, and how
you enforce that is in the harness.
And so if the harness isn't controllable, and having it be open source
is a great way to have it be controllable, but if it isn't controllable, you're
not going to be able to pull those levers efficiently.
And then context as well. Context can come from anywhere.
It can come from pre-existing data sources.
It can come from APIs. It can come from memory that you build up.
And having a harness that works with any sources of context is really important
for being able to own that agent.
We think these agents, in order to own your intelligence, they also need to
be compounding. So what I mean by that is it's pretty easy to build an initial
version of an agent, but almost always that initial version is not what's production
ready enough to ship to millions of users.
And so how do you improve that agent over time?
This is where compounding comes in.
You want the intelligence of that agent to compound over time, whether it's
manually with observability and then noticing things and then fixing
those things, or whether it's automatically in the realm of kind
of like memory.
And then lastly, these agents need to be governed.
This is incredibly important for internal company agents when they're running.
Who do they act on behalf of?
How much is it costing to actually run these?
How do you know what's going on?
Having governance over these agents, and by the way, we think agents will
absolutely transform the operating model of companies out there, but you have
to have governance over them.
You have to know who they're acting on behalf of.
And so we think these three pillars, open, compounding, and governed, are really
the pillars of owning your intelligence.
And when we talk about, like, impacting this at a company, there's not
one thing that you can do to really make this change to owning your intelligence.
It's a combination of things.
And in particular, we think there's three different things.
People process technology.
When we talk about people and how you set a company up for success in terms
of organizing around the idea of owning your intelligence, we think there's
three different rings of personas that are involved in this process.
One is the core GenAI platform team.
These are agent experts. They're standing up the technology and oftentimes
processes for others in the company to benefit from and to use.
Second is all the agent engineers in different business units, and they're
the ones taking these technologies and really making them work for a
particular use case. And then lastly, there's non-technical
builders, non-developers who are absolutely involved in this agent building
process. They're oftentimes the best folks to know what good looks like for
a particular domain or for a particular problem.
And so when you think about owning your intelligence, it really
involves all three of these people.
You need people to set up the core infrastructure.
You need people to build the agents.
And then you need domain experts to really help codify what good or bad
looks like. We think there's certain processes that you're going to want to
implement as well. In particular, we think that building agents is very iterative.
So, as I mentioned, the first version of an agent that you build isn't going
to be the one that's going to serve millions of users successfully.
So you're going to want to spin up this life cycle and really get
this life cycle turning. You're going to want to set up a process where teams
build a version, but then they quickly test it, they quickly deploy it to a
small set of users, they monitor that, and then they take those learnings,
bring them back into build, and really spin this flywheel.
I think the best teams that we see shipping agents, they're the ones who
spin this flywheel as quickly as possible.
And then, of course, there's the technology that powers all of this.
We think there's kind of like two key parts to this technology that
we help people with.
One is the runtime. And so this is how you build and deploy agents.
This includes our open source libraries as well as our deployments.
And then there's observability and eval.
And we think this is core for that kind of like compounding loop.
And so these are pillars of the technology of what we build.
And recently we've been adding a new layer on top as well, which is intelligence.
So everything in the SDLC is getting automated.
And so should agent building.
And so yes, you want to have this flywheel turning, and we want to build a bunch
of tools to make it easy for you as agent engineers to turn that flywheel,
but we also want to build intelligence that helps do parts of this for you
as well. And so when we think of the stack that we're building, we
think of building a runtime.
We think of building this observability and evals and then intelligence on
top to really tie it all together.
And so for the rest of this keynote, I want to talk about these three buckets
and things that we're doing to push the frontier in all of them.
And so I want to start by talking about runtime.
So I said this before, but when we think about building agents, we think
about it in layers. And one layered way to view it is that when you build
agents, there's business logic that goes into a harness that runs on infrastructure.
So business logic includes things like instructions, tools, skills, maybe hooks
to modify some of the harness.
This is stuff that we can never give you.
This is domain-specific stuff that you all or your teammates are experts in
and are going to codify into, again, all of these different things to really
drive the agent in a particular domain or particular use case.
When we talk about the harness, we talk about all of the things around the
model that connect it to external sources of data and computation and context
and business logic. And so we spend a lot of time thinking about this.
What are the right primitives to run the model in and let it really action
on everything that's out there.
And so this is where our open source frameworks come into play.
And in particular, Deep Agents is one that we've released somewhat recently.
It's our newest one. And it's really focused on what this idea of a really
solid base harness looks like.
So it's intended for you to easily modify and easily build on top of, but it
has a lot of primitives that we think are common to how this harness or how
this execution gets done. So in particular, we give it an execution environment.
This can be a file system.
This can be a full-on sandbox.
This can be a lightweight code interpreter.
We do a lot of context management that we've seen just be best practice for
how to work with these models.
So we support skills, memory.
We do summarization when the conversation gets long.
We do context offloading for really large tool calls.
We architect it all in a way that takes advantage of prompt caching.
We add in kind of like ways to steer what the harness is doing.
So we add in human in the loop.
And then we also bake in things like planning and subagents so that you can
spin up small agents to do things.
And so all of these are aspects of a harness that we think are general, and
we provide this off the shelf in Deep Agents, although you can of course
build your own in a more granular way with LangGraph and LangChain.
And then lastly, you've got the infrastructure, and so I think, like,
this is maybe calling out something here.
I don't think the future is just agents running on your laptop just for you.
I think it's agents running in the cloud, working in the background, proactive,
always on, multi-tenant, serving many users.
And so when you think about going from agents that just run locally to
agents that run in the cloud,
there's a whole set of infrastructure that you need in order to make that happen.
You need a runtime for the agent, you need ways that it can connect to tools
in kind of like a properly auth'd and governed way.
You need sandboxes for it to write and execute code in.
And you need an LLM gateway to control how it can access models.
And so you've got all these pieces of infrastructure that are needed.
And we're building a lot of those into LangSmith.
So we have LangSmith Deployments.
This takes your agent, it bundles it up.
It deploys it into a server with streaming and secret storage and the checkpointing
and a task queue. We have a tool server which uses MCP as a protocol and
handles auth and has an audit log on it.
We've got sandboxes where you can write and execute code.
It's got a secrets proxy, so credentials never get in the sandbox, so the agent
can't kind of like see them.
And then we have an LLM gateway for reliability, with fallbacks
and cost controls on it. And so we have all these individual pieces in LangSmith,
and one of the things that we're doing to really make this building experience
faster for folks is bundling it all up into what we call Managed Deep Agents.
So Managed Deep Agents basically combines two of those layers into one.
It combines the harness layer and the managed infrastructure layer into one.
Means instead of... previously you might define your business logic, choose
your harness, and then choose your four or five different pieces of infrastructure,
now you just define your business logic and use Managed Deep Agents, and it's
all bundled in one. We think this makes it really really easy to go from your
business logic to something that's running in production on the web, multi-tenant,
in a scalable way. And so I want to highlight three different
kind of like aspects of Managed Deep Agents that we think are really impactful
for getting time to value.
First, we think that it has a lot of these things built in that help you build
fast. So when you're building fast for a multi-tenant agent, a lot of work,
yes, goes into the context engineering side of things, but a lot of work also
goes into how you connect to things safely.
And so tools, channels, and then the auth associated with those are
really important and really painstaking to set up.
And so by channels, I mean how the agent is triggered.
Is it triggered in Slack? Is it triggered in Teams?
Is it listening to new emails?
Is it listening to new GitHub events?
And so we take all of those in Managed Deep Agents.
We provide off-the-shelf integrations that also handle auth for those.
It's also very easy to deploy this outside of your computer.
So again, it runs in the cloud.
We've separated the agent runtime from the sandbox.
And so there's two different patterns of kind of like running agents that require
kind of like sandboxing in production.
One is you run them in the sandbox.
We think a better pattern is actually to run the agent outside the sandbox
and connect to the sandbox as a tool.
And so we do that, and we bundled it all up into a single kind of like CLI command,
mda deploy.
And then lastly, there's a lot of things that make it easy to govern these
agents at scale. We've seen these agents be really really useful for internal
company agents to transform what the companies look like internally.
When you do this, you need to have a lot of governance around those agents.
So who is this agent acting as?
Maybe it's acting as itself.
Maybe it's acting on behalf of whoever is using it.
What permissions does it have?
What tools can it call into?
What models can it use? How much can this agent spend?
Data that comes into it.
How is that being protected?
Tracing and eval is really important for knowing what's going on and then measuring
the impact of this agent.
And so all of these are bundled into Managed Deep Agents, and we think make
it pretty fast and uniquely differentiated in terms of what it takes
to get started building agents.
This is a little diagram of everything that's kind of like involved.
And so again, we think people are going to be building multi-tenant
applications that interact with the agent.
We think this agent is going to be exposed through a bunch of different interfaces,
UI, Slack, Teams, GitHub. It's going to be running on its own deployment, but
it's going to be connected to sandboxes.
Access to models is going to be running through a gateway.
It's going to be tracing to an observability platform that's going
to be powering evals. And then memory is going to need to be stored somewhere
as well. And so we try to bundle all of this up into Managed Deep Agents.
As I mentioned, we think this is really impactful for internal agents that
are transforming what companies look like.
We think that there'll be a lot of these.
We think that you'll have a lot of business users inside the company
being the best people to build these.
And so we want to make that as easy as possible.
And again, we think this needs to be really governed.
And so we think that we can provide that in this managed agent harness.
These are a few examples of things that we've built internally.
The two biggest ones that I'll call out are Open SWE, which is a coding agent.
So this isn't just helping write code.
It's also helping review code, triage incidents, and in the future
do things like QA. This actually is open source.
The second one that we use a lot internally is GTM Agent.
This is not open source yet, but this powers a lot of our go-to-market operations
from marketing and sales and outreach.
It's a proactive agent, so it's always on.
It's pinging you with updates.
Pinged me to tell me that I had a big conference today.
So thank you very much for that.
And it empowers a lot of what our go-to-market team uses and
does. And so, diving into that a little bit more.
Some of the things it can do are research.
It can do outreach across a bunch of different domains.
And again, this is why connectors are so important.
It can create artifacts. And so these are created in the sandbox.
And then in the sandbox, we expose URLs where you can view them.
And again, it's very much kind of like an autonomous
agent in that it's running not just when you message it, but on all of these
kind of like automations.
And so this is a little bit of like roughly what it looks like.
Again, lots of events coming in, the core agent runtime.
Governance is a key piece and then connections into external systems.
And so this type of internal company agent that's deeply integrated knows
a lot of your business context.
We think this is a glimpse into the future of what future companies
will look like when they're running, and we think Managed Deep Agents will
power a lot of that.
The second big thing I want to talk about is observability and eval.
So we think this is really core for spinning this loop.
We think this loop is really important to get running, and we think traces sit
at the center of this, and so we invest a lot in traces and thinking about
what they look like, and we think agent traces are a new type of data.
They're deeply nested. You've got really large payloads.
You've got different query patterns than before, and you've got a bunch of different
modalities. And we also think they're valuable in different ways.
We think these traces contain natural language, and that natural language contains
things like user intent and logic failures and glimpses into how people
are using the agent, whether it's properly or improperly.
And so LangSmith, of course, is our platform really built around this idea of
agent traces and agent observability and eval.
At the core of LangSmith is SmithDB.
SmithDB is a database that we built internally to be really good at handling
agent traces. It's really performant across a bunch of different dimensions.
And so all of these are different query patterns that we think are relevant
for dealing with traces.
And when we think about SmithDB and therefore LangSmith as a platform,
we want to make it the best agent platform, the best data lake for these
agent traces. And so we think about how agent traces are different and
we think about the different dimensions that you're going to want to ingest
traces on and store traces on and query traces on and visualize traces, like
how is doing all of these things different for agent traces compared to normal
observability or normal data.
We spend a ton of time thinking about that, and so I want to touch on these
four axes because this is a big part of where we're innovating in LangSmith.
And so the first is ingest.
When you ingest agent traces, they contain a bunch of these natural language
clues that you can use to tell how the system is behaving, what people are
using it for, how the agent's responding.
All of these can be encoded in kind of like online evals that you use LLM or
code to judge. And recently there's been a really big improvement to
how you can do this. So previously you would use frontier models for a lot
of these judges. But recently Jev and other decision models have kind of
like emerged as a way to do this more cheaply and more efficiently.
So what is Jev? Jev is the decision model.
What does that mean? It basically means that instead of generating text, it
makes decisions. So you pass in the state and then you pass in a list of questions
with different answers to those questions, and the model basically chooses
the answers, and this makes it really really fast and really really cheap.
And so when you use Jev as a judge, which is a new option that you can use
in LangSmith, you can build quickly.
So it has, like, these standard kind of like answer types that are pretty intuitive
to choose from. You can provide different choices and you can provide different
scores for it to kind of like judge.
So there's a variety of different dimensions that you can use Jev to score
on. And so this is available in LangSmith today.
We think this is a great example of how the ingestion of agent data is different
from kind of like traditional logs.
There are so many clues in the natural language of these agent traces that
you want to score, and things like decision models we think are a great step
forward in doing that reliably.
Next, I want to talk about storing the data.
So SmithDB is where we store the data.
One big difference between kind of like agent traces and traditional logs is
that there's a ton of sensitive data that is in these traces.
So we think a lot about how to best store these traces to deal with
the fact that there's so much sensitive data there.
So we have very flexible hosting of SmithDB and LangSmith.
So we run it in the cloud, obviously, but you can also run it on-prem or in a
new model we have called Bring Your Own Cloud, BYOC, where all the data remains
with you but the control plane lives with us.
One of the things that we've added recently is RBAC on inputs or outputs.
So what does this mean? You've got an agent trace.
You might want engineers to see the skeleton of the trace, the kind
of like tools that were called, the tokens, the latency, so they can see overall
system health, but you don't want them to see the inputs or outputs because
that's where sensitive data could be.
And so we added a new RBAC permission where you can control whether people
can see those inputs or outputs or not.
And then coming up soon as well is more granular ABAC permissions.
So what this will mean is that you can tag traces with different
metadata and then you can set kind of like policies where only certain people
or certain groups of people can see those traces.
This will basically give you much more fine-grained access to who can see which
types of traces. This type of, like, RBAC and ABAC is not usually something
that I see people getting excited about, but it is so key for dealing with this
sensitive information that's in all these traces.
We also think about the right format in which to store these traces.
And so one of the things that we launched recently and improving upon is
LangSmith Trajectories. What is LangSmith Trajectories?
So LangSmith Trajectories is a new format for storing traces.
We visualize it in this very kind of like user-friendly way.
You can still click into things and click around and actually click into things
even more and see all the raw details.
But by default we present it in this kind of like list of messages
way. So trajectories are basically a list of messages, and what that does is
it gives you a standardized format to view traces and also interact with traces.
So the standardized format makes it much faster to debug because you're
now viewing things in kind of like a very simple standardized way.
It makes it simpler to annotate.
So you can bring subject matter experts into the platform.
This is now a much more user-friendly way for them to view that, and they can
annotate there. And then this is also the same format, or it's a very similar
format to what's used in post-training of models.
So we think it makes it ready for that.
Next I want to talk about querying.
So this data is kind of like a new... or it's very text-based.
There's a lot of text in it.
There's a lot of multimodal data in it.
And when we think about kind of like searching for data within these traces,
it presents new challenges compared to traditional
data. So you're...
All of this data contains how people are using your agent, and most of them
are probably using it in standard ways, but there's probably a few that are
using it in, like, weird ways.
And so it's really about finding these needles in a haystack where the way
that they're using it, it's not going to show up in kind of like logs.
It's going to show up in the semantics of how people are using it, where the
errors that happen aren't going to show up in logs.
They're going to happen...
They're going to show up in the semantics.
And so we've added different ways to kind of like search
this data to date. So we have full text search, we have ways of basically filtering
on metadata and filtering on these large payloads, all of which are kind
of like unique problems for agent data.
But I'm really excited about this new way of filtering, which we're calling
kind of like AI Search or AI Query.
And so what this does, and let me flip to a video of this.
So what this does is you can enter in a natural language query right there.
So AI Search, you can type in something in natural language that you want to
see. So, user got confused by agent response, and then under the hood what we're
doing is we're streaming back results, and in real time we're running them through
a decision model. So I talked about these decision models, but we're running
it through a decision model and giving it a confidence of how it meets
that option. We're actually highlighting the places in here where there's evidence
for this. So again, this is not transforming natural language into a
structured query. It's actually taking that prompt and running it as a prompt
over all... You can pair this with other filters, but it's running it
very quickly and efficiently over all results that come back.
And so this is an example of how we're embedding more AI into the platform
to help with the analysis of this special type of data, this special type of
agent trace data. And then lastly, I want to talk about visualization of this data.
So again, this is a new type of data.
How do we think about visualizing it?
We've already seen a little bit of it with this trajectory
view. But one of the things that we've consistently heard is that because
agents operate in so many different domains and there might be different ways
of viewing or interacting with this data in different domains, you also
need different ways to review it in LangSmith.
And so that's why we launched LangSmith Custom Apps.
And I think we have a video here as well, but you can see this is a completely
vibe-coded, completely custom HTML front end.
You can edit it in the UI by going into this vibe coding app, giving
it a prompt. And so here, typing in how you want it to change in natural
language. And you can see that it's doing some work on the right.
We've got an agent in the back end.
It's exploring files. It's trying to figure out what to do.
And now it adds in this other part of the UI, which is visualized
on the right. This is then saved as a view that anyone in the organization
can come in and use. And so we've consistently heard that people
have specific ways that they want to view legal data or finance data, and they
might be vibe coding UIs outside of LangSmith, and that's fine.
But we think by bringing it into the UI, we can let people
do this in a more governed way, where it knows all of the different
APIs. We actually open sourced our design system, so it will look consistent
with the other parts of LangSmith.
And then it just exists in your workspace as a new page that you can
go in and look at.
And so these are all ways that we think about making LangSmith the best
kind of like data platform for trace data.
And then lastly, I want to talk about intelligence.
This is one of the key parts that we are working on in order to
help people get more value out of everything in LangSmith because, yes, great,
there's all this information that's in traces, but how do you action on it?
The visibility over the traces at this point has become table stakes.
Finding issues is really hard.
There's, again, it's finding needles in a haystack.
Understanding issues is hard.
You've got these large traces.
Yes, we're condensing it into trajectories.
And so you can kind of see how things kind of like come together here.
But it's still kind of like understanding issues is hard, and then fixing
issues is hard. And so great, there's some wrong output, but how do you know
whether it's going wrong in the prompt or the context or the model or the retrieval?
And then once you fix it, how do you avoid playing
whack-a-mole, where you kind of fix it once, but then it pops up again
in two months because you change the prompt in a different way.
And so when we think of trying to do this, you do this in a manual
way by spinning this flywheel.
But we launched LangSmith Engine a few months ago as a way to do this
in a more automated way. And so LangSmith Engine we think of as a proactive
agent engineer. It runs in the background on top of traces.
It monitors these issues. It clusters them and diagnoses them.
It proposes fixes via a PR.
It then creates other tests, so it can create data points and create evals,
and then if it's hooked into deployments, it can actually trigger a
deployment from there as well.
And so we're constantly working on this, and so Engine v2 we launched about
a week ago, and it has a bunch of different improvements and new capabilities.
So one of the new capabilities is that it will actually test its
fixes proactively. So this only works if you're running on LangSmith
Deployments. But one of the things that we do in LangSmith Deployments is we
take the changes that we make.
We then basically spin up a new preview deployment and then test that
preview deployment to see if the issues that we found previously now no longer
